doc.title: Ed Soph interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 9, 2024

title: Choosing cymbals; Joey Baron
summary: Cymbals for big band versus small group, drummers bringing their own cymbals, and Joey Baron's different attitude.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Exactly. Yeah. Yeah there’s all sorts of things that, oh I mean you open a real can of worms — that’s why drummers have so many cymbals, unless they’re the leader of the band and can pick you know. But I mean the cymbals that you use for a big band probably you’re not going to use for a small group, although Buddy Rich would kick me for saying that because when you’re in a big band, when you play behind a soloist it immediately becomes a small group. But in the case of say if I’m playing in a guitar trio I have the cymbal sound in my ear that I think will go best with that kind of timbre.
So when I see drummers, if you’re coming from out of town and you book a concert like you have to have a drumset for me, but they come in carrying their cymbal bag.
And do you suppose they have chosen those cymbals particularly for that gig usually?

I don’t know it’s usually just something that — to have one’s own cymbals when playing strange drums is a very important comforting mechanism, and especially ‘cause it’s — drums you can, yeah, you can get by fixing them pretty easily. But if you’ve got bad cymbals it just doesn’t work.
That’s right. You can’t tune a cymbal, right?
Unless you have that ball peen hammer.

Right. I only know of one drummer who likes playing on cymbals he’s never played on before. He’s a great drummer, a great musician, Joey Baron. Joey welcomes it because he says, “Every time I play on a different kit with different cymbals it forces me to play in a
different way. And man I just like — wow. Yes. Definitely. So you know there’s a positive side to everything.
